title: Attribution Epistemology
equation: Attribution Epistemology = Measured Confidence ÷ Experiment-Verified Confidence
hook: Your dashboard says Instagram drove that sale. Your dashboard doesn't actually know that.
statement: You never fully know what caused a conversion, so don't act like you do.
explainer: Dashboards show what happened around the same time, not what caused it. Scale spend on a hunch dressed up as data and you can burn a lot of money fast.
sop: List the 3 growth drivers you're most sure about.
Ask if each belief came from a real test or just dashboard correlation.
Score Measured Confidence and Experiment-Verified Confidence 1 to 10 for each.
Pause or halve one channel you 'know' works and watch revenue.
Hold off scaling anything with a big gap between the two scores.
equation_example: Measured Confidence from your dashboard is 9. Experiment-Verified Confidence from an actual holdout test is 4. 9 ÷ 4 = 2.25. Anything above 1 means you're more sure than the evidence supports. Close to 1 means you've earned it.
question: Write down the channel you're most sure is working, then how you'd actually prove it.
closing_statement: Correlation looks a lot like cause until you test it.
caption:
Principle Nº 96: Attribution Epistemology

Your dashboard says Instagram drove that sale. Your dashboard doesn't actually know that.

You never fully know what caused a conversion, so don't act like you do.

Your turn: Write down the channel you're most sure is working, then how you'd actually prove it.
